zero-trust.s: A security principle that trusts nothing from the start and checks every time someone connects
zero-trust.b: Zero Trust checks the person, the device and the situation each time, whether or not the connection comes from inside the company. Only then does it allow as much access as is needed. It is summed up in the phrase "Never Trust, Always Verify."
zero-trust.tg: Zero Trust is a principle, not a product name. Trust Gateway is SYINNOVATION's solution, developed by applying this principle.

zta.s: A structure that puts the Zero Trust principle into a real system
zta.b: It has two parts: a policy decision part that judges who is trying to access what, and an enforcement part that opens and closes connections according to that decision. The US NIST SP 800-207 document is the best-known reference.

implicit-trust.s: Trusting someone just because they are inside the corporate network
implicit-trust.b: Traditional security treated everything inside the firewall as safe and allowed internal access easily. Zero Trust starts by removing this implicit trust.

least-privilege.s: The principle of giving only as much access as the work truly needs
least-privilege.b: Instead of opening every system, it allows only the systems and functions needed for each person's job. If an account is stolen, this can limit the scope of the damage.

assume-breach.s: A principle of designing as if you may already have been breached
assume-breach.b: It assumes an attacker may already be inside. Each segment is checked separately and every connection is logged, so that if one place is breached, the damage does not spread.

continuous-verification.s: Checking continuously while someone is connected, not just once at login
continuous-verification.b: If the device status, location or behavior changes during a connection, the access decision is made again. This is needed to catch takeover or misuse that happens after login.
continuous-verification.tg: Trust Gateway checks access again at every moment, even after authentication.

micro-segmentation.s: Dividing networks and systems into small pieces so that traffic cannot move freely between them
micro-segmentation.b: If one zone is breached, it keeps the problem from spreading to other zones. It is a common way to reduce lateral movement.

ztna.s: An access method that opens only permitted applications, not the whole network
ztna.b: Unlike a VPN, it does not let users into the whole internal network. It connects users who pass the checks only to the systems they need. It is the approach the financial sector considers first when adopting Zero Trust.
ztna.tg: Trust Gateway's access control for employees works this way.

sdp.s: A design that hides a service so it cannot even be seen until the checks are passed
sdp.b: From outside, no one can see that the server exists or which ports are open, which makes targets hard to find. It is one of the common ways to implement ZTNA.

pdp.s: The "brain" that decides whether to allow a connection
pdp.b: It gathers information about the user, the device and the situation, and decides by policy whether to allow, deny or ask for an extra check. The decision is passed to the Policy Enforcement Point.
pdp.tg: Trust Gateway's policy engine is made up of the Prohibited Conditions check and the Final Decision step. The Prohibited Conditions check gives its opinion, the Final Decision step decides whether to allow access, and the Control Center carries out that decision.

pep.s: The gate that opens and closes connections according to the decision
pep.b: It sits between users and business systems and lets through only the requests the Policy Decision Point has allowed. A gateway or proxy plays this role.
pep.tg: Trust Gateway's Access Gateway is the Policy Enforcement Point. Every request is checked at this point, and step-up authentication is done through approval in the phone app. The PC agent keeps access on hold until the approval is complete.

pip.s: The source that provides the data and attributes needed for a decision
pip.b: It provides data and attributes about users, devices and behavior so that the Policy Decision Point can decide correctly.
pip.tg: Trust Gateway's machine learning Anomaly Detection calculates how much this request differs from the usual pattern. It passes the result to the Policy Decision Point, together with other inputs for the decision such as the Risk Score, location and device security status.

policy-engine.s: The component that turns access rules into actual decisions
policy-engine.b: It applies rules such as "this department gets only this system" or "deny if there is no phone check" to every request. It must be able to apply rule changes right away.

ztmm.s: A framework that measures, in stages, how far an organization has implemented Zero Trust
ztmm.b: The model published by the US CISA is the best-known example. It assesses identity, devices, networks, applications and data stage by stage. It is used to plan adoption and track progress.

attack-surface.s: All the points an attacker could target
attack-surface.b: Ports open to the outside, public services, accounts and devices are all part of the attack surface. The smaller it is, the harder an attack becomes.

lateral-movement.s: An attacker who got into one place moving on to other internal systems
lateral-movement.b: If systems inside the corporate network can reach each other easily, a small intrusion can grow into a major incident. Least privilege and segmentation are used to stop it.

insider-threat.s: Risk caused by internal users who have access rights
insider-threat.b: It includes not only intentional acts but also mistakes and stolen accounts. This is why internal access must also be checked each time.

authentication.s: Checking that the person connecting is really who they claim to be
authentication.b: Identity is proven with means such as a password, a phone or biometric data. What the person can do after that is decided by authorization.

authorization.s: Deciding what a verified user is allowed to do
authorization.b: Even within the same company, the systems and functions an employee can see depend on their job. It is the step after authentication.

idp.s: A service that manages user accounts and logins in one place
idp.b: Instead of each system managing passwords itself, systems trust and use the identity provider's verification result. A company account system is a typical example.

mfa.s: Authentication that uses two or more different kinds of methods
mfa.b: It combines two or more of these: something you know (a password), something you have (a phone or a certificate) and something you are (a fingerprint or face). It can protect the account even if the password leaks.

2fa.s: Authentication that adds one more check after the password
2fa.b: It is multi-factor authentication that uses two steps. Text messages, app notifications and one-time passwords are common.

step-up.s: Asking for an extra check only when something looks risky
step-up.b: Most of the time it lets users through easily. It asks for one more check only when risk is high, such as an unfamiliar device or a sensitive task. It is a way to keep both convenience and security.
step-up.tg: Trust Gateway asks for one more check on the phone when risk rises.

biometric.s: Authentication that uses physical traits such as fingerprints or the face
biometric.b: It is convenient because it cannot be forgotten or lent to someone. Keeping the biometric data on the device and never sending it to a server is the safer approach.

passkey.s: Logging in with a cryptographic key on the device instead of a password
passkey.b: At login, the device creates a signature and sends it, so no password is stored on the server. It is based on the FIDO2 standard and is resistant to phishing.

otp.s: A short numeric password that can be used only once
otp.b: It becomes invalid after a set time or after one use. Codes received by text message are vulnerable to interception, so an app or a dedicated device is safer.

sso.s: Using several systems with a single login
sso.b: It is convenient for users, and administrators can manage accounts in one place. In return, that single login must be protected more strongly.

oauth.s: A standard for delegating access to another service without handing over a password
oauth.b: It issues an access token limited to the scope the user agreed to, so another service can access resources on the user's behalf. It is widely used for social login and external integrations.

oidc.s: A standard built on OAuth 2.0 that tells services who has logged in
oidc.b: It delivers the login result as an ID token, so several services can use the same account. It is often used to set up single sign-on.

saml.s: A standard for exchanging authentication information, long used for enterprise single sign-on
saml.b: The identity provider sends its verification result to each service as a signed document. It is still widely used to connect internal business systems.

jwt.s: A token format that carries user information in a short signed string
jwt.b: A server can check that it is genuine from its signature, without looking up a database each time. If it is stolen, it can be used until it expires, so its validity period is kept short.

session.s: The state kept while a user stays connected after login
session.b: The server and browser remember the state so the user does not have to log in again for every request. If session information leaks, someone else can pick it up and keep using it.

device-binding.s: Tying an account or certificate to a specific device
device-binding.b: Login or access works only from the registered device. Authentication data moved to another device can no longer be used.
device-binding.tg: Trust Gateway binds each certificate to the device it was issued to, so it cannot be used if it is moved to another device.

passwordless.s: Logging in with a device or biometric data instead of a password
passwordless.b: It reduces the risks of password leaks, password reuse and phishing. Passkeys and app approval are typical examples.

two-device.s: Verifying with a PC and a phone together
two-device.b: When an access request comes from a PC, the registered phone is used to confirm again that it is really you. Stealing only one of the two devices is not enough to get in.
two-device.tg: Trust Gateway uses Multi-Signal Cross Check to compare signals from the PC, the phone and the network, and checks whether the same person is in the same place.

multi-signal.s: A way of checking that compares several signals from different sources to find contradictions
multi-signal.b: It looks at location, Wi-Fi, time of day, device status and network information together. One signal can be faked, but it is hard to make all of the signals match at the same time.
multi-signal.tg: Trust Gateway compares the signals collected from the PC, the phone and the network against each other to find combinations that do not add up.

trust-auth.s: SYINNOVATION's phone authentication app, used together with Trust Gateway
trust-auth.b: On iOS and Android, it handles access approval and identity verification. It is also provided as an SDK that customers can build into their own apps.

integrated-auth.s: Bringing identity verification for several services under one authentication technology
integrated-auth.b: Instead of each app building its own authentication, they all use the same common authentication. This makes management easier and keeps the security level even across services.
integrated-auth.tg: Trust Gateway's integrated authentication is a mobile authentication technology that is in operation in the authentication services of card companies and savings banks.

encryption.s: Transforming data so it cannot be read without the right key
encryption.b: It is used both for data in transit and for stored data. Managing the keys safely is the core of encryption.

public-key.s: Encryption and signing with a pair of keys: a public key and a private key
public-key.b: What is locked with a public key can be opened only with its matching private key. It is the technology behind certificates and TLS.

private-key.s: A secret key that only its owner should hold
private-key.b: It is used to create signatures and to decrypt data. If it leaks, anyone can pose as that identity, so it is kept in secure storage on the device.

hash.s: Turning data into a fixed-length value that works like a fingerprint
hash.b: If the original changes even slightly, the value changes completely, so tampering can be detected. The original cannot be worked out backward from the hash value.

digital-signature.s: A signature made with a private key that proves who wrote something and whether it was changed
digital-signature.b: The receiver checks the signature with the public key to learn who sent it and whether it was changed on the way. It is used in certificates and in software distribution.

pki.s: A system that issues and manages certificates so that public keys can be trusted
pki.b: It consists of certificate authorities, certificates, revocation lists and management policies. It is the basis for verifying the identity of devices and people with certificates.

ca.s: The party that issues certificates and vouches for the identity in them
ca.b: Only certificates signed by a certificate authority can be trusted. Some organizations run their own internal certificate authority.

root-cert.s: The top-level certificate where trust begins
root-cert.b: Every other certificate must chain back to it to be trusted. The root's private key is stored under the strictest protection.

intermediate-cert.s: A certificate that links the root certificate to the certificates actually in use
intermediate-cert.b: Certificates are issued at an intermediate level so that the root key is not used every day. If a problem occurs, only the intermediate certificate needs to be replaced.

x509.s: An electronic document, signed by a certificate authority, that contains a public key and information about its owner
x509.b: It contains a name, a public key, a validity period and the issuer's signature. It is the standard used to verify the identity of websites and devices.

csr.s: A request sent to a certificate authority asking it to issue a certificate
csr.b: The device creates its own key pair and sends only the public key, so the private key never leaves the device.
csr.tg: Trust Gateway issues the certificate bound to the device that sent this request.

revocation.s: Making a certificate unusable while it is still within its validity period
revocation.b: When a device is lost or has become risky, trust is withdrawn right away. The revocation is announced through a revocation list or a status check.
revocation.tg: Trust Gateway revokes the certificate of a phone that has become risky.

crl.b: The certificate authority publishes it regularly, and the checking side rejects any certificate on the list. As the list grows, a status check method is used alongside it.

ocsp.s: A way to ask right away whether a single certificate is currently valid
ocsp.b: Instead of downloading the whole revocation list, it looks up only the certificate needed. Responses are fast, so it suits real-time checks.

cert-lifecycle.s: The whole process of issuing, renewing and revoking a certificate
cert-lifecycle.b: Missing an expiry date stops a service, and revoking too late leaves risk behind. This is why systematic management matters.
cert-lifecycle.tg: Trust Gateway's PC certificates are valid only for a short time, and each time a new one is issued, it goes through approval again.

device-cert.s: A certificate that proves the identity of a device, not a person
device-cert.b: It is used to check whether a device is a registered company device. The private key is kept in secure storage on the device, which makes it hard to copy.

tls.s: A standard that encrypts internet traffic and verifies the server on the other end
tls.b: The https in a web address means TLS is in use. It keeps others from snooping on or changing what is sent.

mtls.s: TLS in which not only the server but also the connecting side proves itself with a certificate
mtls.b: Regular TLS proves only the server. With mutual TLS, the user's device must also present a certificate to connect, so unregistered devices are filtered out right at the connection stage.
mtls.tg: Trust Gateway sets up mutual TLS connections with device certificates.

key-store.s: Storage in the operating system that keeps private keys and certificates safe
key-store.b: The Windows certificate store, the macOS Keychain and a phone's secure storage are typical examples. They keep apps from freely taking keys out.

key-attestation.s: Proving that a cryptographic key was created inside the security hardware of a real device
key-attestation.b: It can filter out keys created on emulators or in cloned environments. Android and iOS each provide this kind of feature.
key-attestation.tg: Trust Gateway checks key attestation on Android devices.

hsm.s: A dedicated device that creates and stores cryptographic keys safely
hsm.b: It handles signing and encryption without the keys ever leaving the device. It is used to store the most important keys of certificate authorities and financial systems.

secure-enclave.t: Secure Enclave and Trusted Execution Environment (TEE)
secure-enclave.s: A secure execution area on a device, separated from ordinary apps
secure-enclave.b: Biometric data and cryptographic keys are processed here, so they can stay protected even if the operating system is compromised.

ip-address.s: The address used to find a device on a network
ip-address.b: Even for the same person, the address changes between home, the office and a mobile network. That is why trusting a person based on the IP address alone is risky.

port.s: A number that identifies a service within a single device
port.b: Each service uses a set number. The web, for example, usually uses 443. The more ports are open to the outside, the larger the attack surface.

tcp.s: A way of communicating that ensures all data arrives complete and in order
tcp.b: Most internet services, such as the web and email, use it. It sets up and confirms the connection, which makes it highly reliable.

udp.s: A way of communicating that cuts confirmation steps to send data quickly
udp.b: It is used where speed matters, such as video calls, games and some VPNs. It does not resend missing data, but in return it has less delay.

http2.s: A web protocol that sends and receives many requests at the same time over a single connection
http2.b: It does not need to open many connections, so it is fast and efficient. Most web services today use it.
http2.tg: Trust Gateway's access to web-based work systems runs over HTTP/2 connections.

https.b: The padlock in the address bar means HTTPS is in use. Sensitive data such as logins and payments must always be sent over HTTPS.

dns.s: The internet's address book that turns domain names into IP addresses
dns.b: People find things by name, and devices by numeric address. If DNS is tampered with, users can be led to fake sites.

proxy.s: An intermediate server that passes requests between users and servers on their behalf
proxy.b: It is used to log or filter access. Placed on the user side, it is called a forward proxy. Placed on the server side, it is called a reverse proxy.

reverse-proxy.s: A relay server in front of servers that receives requests and passes them to the servers inside
reverse-proxy.b: It handles authentication, encryption and load balancing in one place, without exposing the servers inside directly.

reverse-connection.s: A setup in which the server inside connects outward first and keeps that connection open
reverse-connection.b: The company can receive outside requests without opening inbound ports in its firewall. This removes the entry point that attackers would target.
reverse-connection.tg: Trust Gateway's Internal Agent only connects outward, so there is no need to open inbound ports.

gateway.s: A gate that controls traffic between different networks
gateway.b: It checks incoming and outgoing requests and sends them to the right place. In Zero Trust, it acts as the Policy Enforcement Point.

firewall.s: A device that allows or blocks network traffic according to set rules
firewall.b: It filters traffic based on addresses and ports. Because it cannot tell people and devices apart, Zero Trust uses it together with other ways of checking.

waf.s: A firewall that inspects the content of web requests and filters out attacks
waf.b: It looks for web attack patterns such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting (XSS). It checks even the content of requests, which a regular firewall cannot see.

vpn.s: A way to connect to the internal network through an encrypted tunnel over the internet
vpn.b: Once connected, users can reach a wide range of systems, as if they were inside the internal network. So if a single account is stolen, the damage can be large.
vpn.tg: Trust Gateway connects users only to the work systems they need, instead of using a VPN.

ipsec.s: A standard that encrypts traffic at the network layer
ipsec.b: It is often used for VPNs that link company branch offices. It tends to be complex to set up.

ssl-vpn.s: A remote access VPN that uses TLS encryption
ssl-vpn.b: Users connect to the internal network through a browser or a dedicated app. Because the access appliance is exposed to the internet, its vulnerabilities are a frequent target of attacks.

wireguard.s: A VPN tunnel technology built with compact code and modern cryptography
wireguard.b: It is simple to set up, fast, and has less code to review.

tunneling.s: A technique that wraps one kind of traffic inside another to send it
tunneling.b: It creates an encrypted tunnel so that no one in between can see the contents. A VPN is a typical example.

relay.s: Passing traffic through an intermediate server when a direct connection is hard
relay.b: When a firewall or the network environment blocks a direct connection, a relay is used to get around it. It is a fallback that keeps the connection from dropping.

nat.s: A technology that lets many devices share one public IP address
nat.b: Most home and office routers use it. It also makes it hard to connect directly from outside to a device inside.

inbound-outbound.s: Traffic coming in and traffic going out
inbound-outbound.b: In security, blocking incoming traffic is the baseline. Allowing outgoing traffic only to set destinations is also becoming common.

latency.s: The time it takes from sending a request to getting a response
latency.b: More security checks can mean more delay, so a design that handles the checks quickly is important.

load-balancer.s: A device that spreads requests across multiple servers
load-balancer.b: It keeps the service running even if one server is overloaded or stops.

api.s: A channel through which programs exchange functions and data in an agreed way
api.b: Apps and servers, and one company's systems and another's, are connected through APIs. Unauthenticated API calls are a common cause of data leaks.

api-gateway.s: A gate in front of many APIs that manages authentication, permissions and call volume
api-gateway.b: Instead of each service checking on its own, it handles these checks consistently in one place.

sdk.s: A bundle of development tools that lets a feature be added to another company's app
sdk.b: Common features such as authentication can be added instead of being built again for each app.
sdk.tg: Trust Auth's authentication features are also provided as an SDK that can be built into customers' apps.

ssh.s: Encrypted communication for connecting to a server remotely and running commands
ssh.b: Because it is an essential tool for managing servers, it is also a frequent target of attacks. Who can connect, and from which devices, should be strictly limited.

rdp.s: A feature for using another computer's screen remotely
rdp.b: It is widely used for remote work and remote support. But if it is left directly open to the internet, it becomes a major entry path for ransomware.

risk-score.s: A number that shows how risky an access attempt or a transaction is
risk-score.b: It is calculated from signals such as the device, location, time and behavior. Depending on the score, the result is to allow, ask for an extra check, or deny.
risk-score.tg: Trust Gateway records the score and the reasons with each decision, so it can explain why it decided as it did.

context.s: Information about who is connecting, with which device, from where and when
context.b: Even for the same account, a context that differs from usual draws more suspicion. It is an input to Zero Trust decisions.

device-posture.s: Checking whether the connecting device is in a safe state
device-posture.b: It checks items such as jailbreaking or rooting, emulator use and security settings. It filters out infected or tampered devices.
device-posture.tg: Trust Gateway checks for jailbreaking or rooting, emulators and debugger use.

jailbreak.s: A state in which the security restrictions of a phone's operating system have been removed
jailbreak.b: Apps can then reach each other's data, which puts financial apps and authentication data at risk. Many financial apps refuse to run on such devices.

emulator.s: A program that imitates a phone on a computer
emulator.b: It is useful for development, but attackers also use it to analyze apps or run automated attacks. That is why checks are made to confirm that it is a real device.

ueba.s: Analysis that learns the usual behavior of users and devices to spot behavior that differs
ueba.b: Access at an unusual time, or to a system the user does not normally use, is treated as a warning sign. It is used to find stolen accounts.

anomaly.s: Finding patterns that differ from the usual
anomaly.b: It sets a normal baseline and flags access or transactions that stray far from it. If the baseline is set wrong, false positives increase.

fds.s: A system that finds unusual transactions in payments and financial transactions
fds.b: It looks at the device, location, amount and transaction pattern to pick out risky transactions. It is a core tool that card companies and banks use to stop fraudulent use.
fds.tg: Trust Gateway detects payment fraud and sends alerts and recommendations (approve, step-up authentication or deny) with the reasons to the client's FDS. It also diagnoses the FDS rules through after-the-fact reports. The customer decides whether to approve or decline a payment.

false-positive.s: Wrongly treating something normal as risky, and missing something that is risky
false-positive.b: Too many false positives inconvenience users, and too many false negatives lead to incidents. Striking a balance between the two is the core of detection design.

audit-log.s: A record of who did what and when
audit-log.b: When an incident happens, it is the basis for tracing the cause and determining responsibility. It can serve as evidence only if it is stored so that it cannot be altered.
audit-log.tg: Trust Gateway records the reasons for every access decision. It links the history of certificate issuance and revocation with hashes, so that any later changes become visible.

hash-chain.s: A structure that links records like a chain by putting the hash of each record into the next one
hash-chain.b: Changing even one record in the middle breaks every hash after it, so forgery can be detected.

siem.s: A system that collects and analyzes security logs from many systems
siem.b: It connects scattered records in one place, finds risky patterns and raises alerts.

soc.s: A team or center that constantly watches the security situation and responds
soc.b: It reviews alerts, decides whether they are real incidents and directs the response.

incident-response.s: The process of reducing damage and recovering when a security incident occurs
incident-response.b: It goes in this order: detection, containment, root cause analysis, recovery and prevention of recurrence. A procedure set in advance makes it possible to move quickly.

explainability.s: Showing the reasons why something was allowed or denied
explainability.b: Staff can review decisions and correct false positives. In the financial sector, it is also needed to respond to regulators.
explainability.tg: Trust Gateway shows the reasons and the score with each decision.

phishing.s: An attack that pretends to be a trusted party to steal information or money
phishing.b: Fake emails, text messages and websites trick people into entering passwords or authentication data. Authentication that relies only on passwords is weak against phishing.

smishing.b: Text messages pretending to be from a delivery company or a public agency contain links that lure people into installing malicious apps or entering information.

ato.s: Taking over someone else's account and using it as if you were that person
ato.b: It happens through leaked passwords, phishing or session hijacking. To stop it, checks must continue even after login.

credential-stuffing.s: An attack that tries account details leaked elsewhere, in large volumes
credential-stuffing.b: People who reuse the same password in many places become victims. Multi-factor authentication and device checks stop it.

brute-force.s: An attack that tries every possible password one by one
brute-force.b: The shorter and simpler the password, the faster it is cracked. Limiting the number of attempts and multi-factor authentication are the basic defenses.

mitm.s: An attack that gets in the middle of a communication to snoop on it or change it
mitm.b: It happens through public Wi-Fi or fake certificates. TLS and certificate checks are the basic defense.

session-hijacking.s: An attack that steals the information of a logged-in session to connect as that user
session-hijacking.b: It targets the session after the password and multi-factor authentication have been passed, so it is hard to stop with login security alone. The device and context must be checked continuously.

replay.s: An attack that resends an intercepted authentication request as is
replay.b: It is stopped with values that can be used only once and with time limits.

ransomware.s: Malware that encrypts data so it cannot be used, then demands money
ransomware.b: Remote access appliances and stolen accounts are the main ways in. Blocking lateral movement and keeping backups separate reduce the damage.

malware.s: A program secretly installed on a device to cause harm
malware.b: It takes many forms, such as stealing information, controlling the device remotely and encrypting data.

ddos.s: An attack that floods a service with requests from many devices at once to bring it down
ddos.b: It makes the service slow down or stop. Defenses that filter out large-scale traffic are needed.

social-engineering.s: An attack that tricks people, not technology, by playing on their psychology to obtain information
social-engineering.b: Attackers pretend to be in a hurry or to be a boss to get passwords or approvals. Checks done by people need to be backed up with technology.

zero-day.s: A vulnerability that is not yet known or has no fix available
zero-day.b: It is hard to block because no patch exists yet. The way to prepare is to reduce exposure and detect abnormal behavior.

supply-chain.s: An attack that reaches its target through software or an outside vendor
supply-chain.b: It comes in through trusted updates or partner accounts. This is why outside access must be checked just like internal access.

network-separation.s: Separating the work network from the internet network to shut out outside threats
network-separation.b: Korea's financial sector has long followed strict network separation. As cloud use and remote work grow, ways to complement it with Zero Trust are being discussed.

fin-zt-guide.t: Zero Trust Security Guide for the Financial Sector
fin-zt-guide.s: A Korean guide that helps financial companies adopt Zero Trust and check their implementation
fin-zt-guide.b: First published in February 2026, it includes examples of ZTNA adoption in the financial sector and items for security assessment.

zt-guideline.s: Korea's guide to adopting Zero Trust, published by the Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT)
zt-guideline.b: Version 2.0 was released in 2024. It explains the core principles and the stages of adoption.

nist-800-207.s: The Zero Trust Architecture standard document from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
nist-800-207.b: It is the leading reference that sets out the concept and components of Zero Trust, and guidelines in many countries are based on it.

efta.s: Korean law that sets rules for the safety of electronic financial transactions and the protection of their users
efta.b: It sets the security duties that financial companies and electronic financial business operators must meet, and their liability for incidents.

efsr.s: Detailed supervisory rules for applying Korea's Electronic Financial Transactions Act in practice
efsr.b: They contain security requirements for the financial sector, such as network separation, authentication and the outsourcing of information processing.

pipa.s: Korean law that sets the rules for collecting, using, storing and destroying personal information
pipa.b: It requires organizations to collect only the information they need, manage it safely and delete it once it is no longer needed.

isms-p.t: Personal Information & Information Security Management System (ISMS-P)
isms-p.s: A Korean scheme that certifies information security and personal information protection management systems together
isms-p.b: It audits whether an organization has a security management system in place and runs it properly, and then certifies it.

identity-verification.s: Confirming through official means that a service user is really that person
identity-verification.b: Methods such as phone-based identity verification and ID card checks are used. It is the starting point for opening accounts and for remote (non-face-to-face) financial transactions.

black-cloud.s: A design that hides even the server's address until the checks are complete
black-cloud.b: Until authentication and authorization are passed, no DNS information or IP address is revealed, so attackers cannot find the target. It is a design approach used in software-defined perimeters.

auth-before-connect.s: Opening a connection only after the checks are finished
auth-before-connect.b: The order is the reverse of the traditional way, which accepts the connection first and checks the login afterward. Unverified connections never even reach the server.

identity-centric.s: Security based on the identity of people and devices, not on network location
identity-centric.b: It looks first at who is connecting and with which device, rather than from where. With the growth of remote work and the cloud, it has become a central idea of Zero Trust.

visibility.s: The ability to see at a glance the state and flow of networks, systems and data
visibility.b: You cannot protect what you cannot see, so you first need to see who connects to what, across every segment. It is the starting point for adopting Zero Trust.

segmentation.s: Dividing networks and systems so that attacks do not spread
segmentation.b: Dividing them logically or separating them physically keeps other areas safe even if one is breached. Micro-segmentation applies this at a finer level.

multi-layered.s: A system that applies different levels of security according to how important the information is (its grade)
multi-layered.b: Instead of keeping all information behind the same wall, it uses networks and controls that match each grade. Korea's National Network Security Framework (N2SF) for the public sector also builds on this concept.

sase.s: An architecture that delivers network and security functions together from the cloud
sase.b: It handles functions such as ZTNA, web security and cloud access control together at cloud locations close to users. It suits organizations with many branch offices and remote workers.

remote-work.s: Protecting work systems and data when people work from home or elsewhere
remote-work.b: Because people use networks outside the company and personal devices, security built around the internal network does not hold. An approach that checks people and devices directly is needed.

legacy-system.s: An older existing system that is hard to add modern security features to
legacy-system.b: It is essential to the business but hard to change, so it easily becomes a weak link in security. It is protected by placing a gateway in front of it that checks access on its behalf.

access-control.s: Deciding who can access what, and making sure that is followed
access-control.b: It includes authentication, authorization and the mechanisms that actually apply the result. It is divided into several models, depending on the criteria used.

rbac.s: Granting permissions based on job or role
rbac.b: Permissions are tied to roles such as "sales team" or "administrator", and people are assigned to roles. It is easy to manage and widely used, but it has trouble handling detailed conditions.

abac.s: Deciding case by case by combining attributes of the user, the resource and the environment
abac.b: It looks at conditions such as department, job level, time, location and device status together. It can express more detailed rules than role-based access control.

pbac.s: Deciding access according to policy rules set in advance
pbac.b: The organization's security policy is written down as rules and applied to every request. When the policy changes, the same standard applies to all systems right away.

mac.s: A method in which the system enforces access decisions based on security levels
mac.b: Users cannot pass on permissions as they like. Access is decided by comparing the level of the information with the level of the person. It is used where levels are strictly managed, such as the military and public agencies.

privilege.s: The right to access and work with a specific resource or function
privilege.b: The broader the privilege, the greater the damage when an incident happens. It should be granted only as much as is needed and managed together with identity verification.

pam.s: A system that separately controls and records accounts with high privileges, such as administrator accounts
pam.b: Because a leaked privileged account can do great damage, each use needs approval and the work is recorded. Sessions are often recorded on video as well.

iam.s: A system that manages user identities and access rights in one place
iam.b: It creates, changes and removes accounts and permissions as people join, move between departments and leave. It is the foundation that Zero Trust is built on.

entity-id.s: Identifying applications, users and devices separately
entity-id.b: Detailed policies can be applied only if you can tell who is using which device and which app. This is what sets it apart from a firewall that looks only at addresses.

execution-control.s: Allowing only approved programs to run
execution-control.b: Programs or scripts that are not on the list are not allowed to run. It is effective against unknown malware.

risk-based-auth.s: Changing the strength of authentication based on how risky the situation is
risk-based-auth.b: The check is simple when the device and place are the usual ones, and stricter in unfamiliar situations. It is used together with step-up authentication.

edr.s: A security tool that finds and responds to threat activity on PCs and servers
edr.b: It watches processes, files and network activity on the device, and blocks and records suspicious behavior.

soar.s: A tool that automatically runs security response procedures one step after another
soar.b: When an alert comes in, it automatically carries out information gathering, blocking and notification in a set order. It speeds up response and reduces repetitive work for staff.

log-management.s: Collecting logs from many systems in one place to store and search them
log-management.b: Scattered records must be gathered in one place so you can follow what happened when an incident occurs. Retention periods and protection against forgery are important.

threat-intelligence.s: Collecting information about attackers and their methods to use for defense
threat-intelligence.b: Known malicious addresses, attack techniques and vulnerability information are fed into detection rules. This helps prepare for similar attacks in advance.

vulnerability.s: A weakness in software or settings that can be exploited in an attack
vulnerability.b: Causes include code defects, wrong settings and outdated versions. Finding them, prioritizing them and fixing them must be done continuously.

cve.s: A standard ID number given to each publicly disclosed vulnerability
cve.b: It lets everyone in the world call the same vulnerability by the same name. It serves as a reference when deciding which patch to apply first.

patch-management.s: Checking for security updates and applying them without missing any
patch-management.b: Most known vulnerabilities can be fixed with patches, but if patching is delayed, systems stay exposed to attacks.

configuration-management.s: Recording system settings and versions and managing changes to them
configuration-management.b: You need to know who changed what and when to find wrong settings and roll them back. It is basic material for security reviews.

dlp.s: Technology that finds sensitive data and stops it from leaking out
dlp.b: It monitors important information leaving through email, messaging apps, file transfers, inputs to generative AI and other channels.

casb.s: A security broker that applies policies between users and cloud services
casb.b: It shows who uses which cloud services and how, and blocks unauthorized use and data leaks.

sbom.s: A list of the components and libraries inside a piece of software
sbom.b: You need to know which open source components and versions are inside to check right away whether a newly found vulnerability affects you.

api-security.s: Authenticating and inspecting API calls to prevent misuse and leaks
api-security.b: As connections between services grow, APIs have become a major attack path. Verifying the identity of the caller and limiting the scope of permissions are the basics.

cia-triad.s: Confidentiality, integrity and availability: the three basic goals of information security
cia-triad.b: Most security measures can be explained by which of these three they aim to protect.

confidentiality.s: Keeping information from being revealed to anyone who is not authorized
confidentiality.b: Encryption and access control are the main ways to protect confidentiality.

integrity.s: Ensuring that information has not been changed without permission
integrity.b: Hashes and digital signatures are used to check for tampering. It is the basis of trust in financial transactions and records.

availability.s: The state in which authorized users can use a system without interruption whenever they need it
availability.b: DDoS attacks and outages harm availability. It is protected with redundancy and load balancing.

data-classification.s: Sorting information into grades by importance and sensitivity
data-classification.b: Each grade gets a different level of protection, so security efforts focus on the most important information.

data-flow-id.s: Attaching identifying information to each data flow to track it
data-flow-id.b: Knowing which data moved from where to where makes it possible to apply policies per flow and to trace incidents.

apt.s: A sophisticated attack that persistently goes after a specific target over a long period
apt.b: After getting in, attackers stay hidden for a long time to steal information or prepare a larger attack. Blocking lateral movement and finding abnormal behavior are important.

ax.s: Reshaping existing work and systems around AI
ax.b: It automates repetitive work and uses data to change how people work. Along the way, handling data and permissions safely becomes just as important.

prompt-injection.s: An attack that uses malicious input to make an AI break its original instructions
prompt-injection.b: It can be done by entering commands directly, or by hiding commands in documents or web pages for the AI to read. It is a leading threat to AI services.

model-jailbreak.s: An attack that gets around an AI model's safeguards to draw out forbidden answers
model-jailbreak.b: It slips past policies through role-play or indirect wording. It is a different concept from jailbreaking or rooting a phone.

llm-guardrail.s: A safeguard that filters the input and output of a large language model to prevent risks
llm-guardrail.b: It filters out problems such as harmful answers, exposure of sensitive information and bypassing of instructions at the input and output stages.

model-extraction.s: An attack that copies an AI model or infers its internals by repeatedly asking questions and collecting the answers
model-extraction.b: It can infringe intellectual property and serve as a stepping stone for other attacks. Limits on call volume and detection of abnormal use help stop it.

adversarial-attack.s: An attack that changes input in ways people cannot notice so that an AI makes wrong decisions
adversarial-attack.b: Small changes to images or data fool classification and detection. When AI is used for security decisions, this must be prepared for as well.

excessive-agency.s: The risk that comes from giving an AI agent more permissions and autonomy than it needs
excessive-agency.b: A manipulated AI could freely carry out actions such as sending emails or deleting files. The principle of least privilege must apply to AI too.

agentic-ai-risk.s: New risks created by AI agents that decide and act on their own
agentic-ai-risk.b: Because they work directly with tools and systems, wrong decisions or manipulation can lead to real damage. Limits on permissions and records of actions are needed.

unbounded-consumption.s: The risk of an AI service's resources being used without limit, causing costs and outages
unbounded-consumption.b: Excessive requests can slow the service down or drive up costs sharply. Limits on call volume and usage monitoring help stop it.

sensitive-disclosure.s: The risk of personal or confidential information leaking through an AI's answers
sensitive-disclosure.b: Information in training data or connected documents can end up mixed into answers. Input and output checks and access rights management are needed.

system-prompt-leakage.s: The risk that instructions hidden in an AI are revealed to users
system-prompt-leakage.b: If internal rules or secrets are put in the instructions, they can leak as is. The rule is to keep sensitive information out of the instructions.

vector-weakness.s: Security weaknesses in the vector stores and embeddings that an AI refers to
vector-weakness.b: Poisoned documents can get mixed in, or documents the user has no right to see can appear in search results. Access rights need to be managed for each document.

hallucination.s: An AI producing convincing content that is not true
hallucination.b: Using such content as is for business decisions can lead to wrong decisions. Showing the source documents alongside the answer and having a person review it are needed.

sovereign-ai.s: Keeping data and AI models under the control of one's own country or organization
sovereign-ai.b: It is a movement to keep sensitive data from going to overseas or outside services. Interest is especially high in the financial and public sectors.

on-device-ai.s: Using AI to find threats on the device itself rather than on a server
on-device-ai.b: It decides right on the device without sending data out, so it is fast and raises fewer privacy concerns.

n2sf.s: Korea's public sector security framework that applies different security according to how important the information is
n2sf.b: The National Intelligence Service (NIS) released it in 2025. Instead of uniform network separation, it sorts information into Classified, Sensitive and Open, and applies security measures that match each grade. It is based on the Zero Trust concept.

security-grade.s: Grades that classify information as Classified (C), Sensitive (S) or Open (O)
security-grade.b: This classification is used in the National Network Security Framework (N2SF), and the level of security measures to apply differs by grade.

security-controls.s: A list of security measures set out to be applied according to each grade
security-controls.b: The National Network Security Framework presents measures grouped by area, such as permissions, authentication, and separation and isolation. Each agency chooses and applies them to fit the nature of its work.

adequacy-assessment.s: The step of assessing whether the security measures applied are enough, and fixing them
adequacy-assessment.b: This is the last step of the National Network Security Framework process. After the measures are applied, it checks whether risk has been reduced enough and adds more where it falls short.

info-service-model.s: A reference model that bundles security measures in advance for common types of work
info-service-model.b: So that agencies do not have to choose every measure from scratch, it presents example security setups that fit each type of work.

risk-tiered.s: Setting different security levels according to the risk of the information and the work
risk-tiered.b: Instead of locking everything down the same way, it protects important areas more strongly and less important areas more flexibly.

osi.s: A reference model that explains network communication in seven layers
osi.b: It divides roles layer by layer, from physical signals up to applications. It is often used to explain which layer a security device looks at.

packet.s: A small bundle of data, split up to be sent over a network
packet.b: Each one carries the sender and receiver addresses and order information. Packets travel separately and are put back together at the end.

packet-loss.s: Some data bundles disappearing during transmission
packet-loss.b: It happens on unstable wireless networks or congested lines, and causes choppy screens and slow responses.

bandwidth.s: The amount of data that can be sent in a given time
bandwidth.b: It is often compared to the number of lanes on a road. Even with wide bandwidth, the connection can feel slow if latency is high.

jitter.s: How uneven the gaps between arriving data are
jitter.b: In real-time communication such as video calls or remote screens, it causes stuttering and delay.

qos.s: A technology that gives priority to important traffic to guarantee its quality
qos.b: When lines are busy, it sends important traffic, such as business calls or payments, first.

router.s: Equipment that decides the path data takes between different networks
router.b: It looks at the destination address and sends packets along the most suitable path.

switch.s: Equipment that connects devices within the same network
switch.b: It connects the PCs, printers and servers in an office, and delivers data only to the device that should receive it.

lan-wan.t: Local Area Network (LAN) and Wide Area Network (WAN)
lan-wan.s: A network covering a small area such as an office, and a network covering a wide area that links regions
lan-wan.b: A LAN is a network within one building or floor. A WAN links places far apart, such as a head office and its branches.

vlan.s: A technology that splits one physical network into several logical networks
vlan.b: Networks can be divided by department or purpose while using the same equipment. It is a basic way to divide internal segments.

subnet.s: A smaller unit of a large network, divided by address range
subnet.b: It groups addresses for management and makes it possible to apply different rules to each segment.

public-private-ip.s: Addresses used on the internet, and addresses used only inside an internal network
public-private-ip.b: A public IP is unique on the internet, while a private IP works only inside a company or home. NAT translates between them.

ipv6.s: The existing and the new internet address systems
ipv6.b: As IPv4 addresses run short, IPv6, which offers far more addresses, is being used alongside it.

dhcp.s: A way to automatically hand out IP addresses to devices that connect
dhcp.b: It means no one has to set the address of each device by hand.

mac-address.s: A unique hardware address given to each network device
mac-address.b: It is used to tell devices apart within the same network. Because it can be changed, it is not enough on its own to trust a device.

cdn.s: A network that sends content from servers close to the user
cdn.b: It delivers web pages and images quickly, and is also used to absorb large-scale traffic attacks.

sd-wan.s: A technology that bundles several lines with software to manage connections between sites
sd-wan.b: It uses dedicated lines and regular internet lines together, and switches paths depending on conditions.

mpls.t: Leased Line and Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS)
mpls.s: A communication line used only to connect specific points
mpls.b: Its quality and security are stable, so it is widely used in the financial sector to connect head offices, branches and outside institutions. It tends to be expensive.

redundancy.s: Having two or more sets of equipment or lines so that service continues if one stops
redundancy.b: It is a basic design for financial systems, whose services must not stop.

high-availability.s: A design that keeps a service running almost without stopping, even when failures occur
high-availability.b: It combines redundancy, automatic failover and load balancing to keep downtime to a minimum.

wifi.s: Wireless LAN that connects devices to a network over radio waves
wifi.b: With public Wi-Fi, you cannot know who runs it, so there is a risk that traffic is snooped on or intercepted.

mobile-network.s: The mobile networks that phones use
mobile-network.b: The connection continues while on the move, but the IP address changes every time the network changes. That is why checking the device and the person, not the address, is the right approach.

handshake.s: The process in which both sides check each other and agree on terms before communication starts
handshake.b: In a TLS handshake, the encryption method is agreed on and the certificate is checked. In mutual TLS, the device certificate is also checked at this point.

cert-pinning.s: A way for an app to trust only a server certificate it has set in advance
cert-pinning.b: It is effective against man-in-the-middle attacks that use fake certificates. Financial apps use it widely.

quic.s: A new transport method that connects quickly and securely over UDP
quic.b: Connections take less time to set up, and they rarely drop when the network changes.

websocket.s: A way of communicating in which the server and browser keep exchanging data after connecting once
websocket.b: It is used where the server needs to send data first, such as notifications, chat and live screens.

rest-api.s: A way of designing APIs that exchange resources using web addresses and HTTP methods
rest-api.b: It is simple and easy to understand, so most web service integrations use it.

cloud.s: Renting servers and software over the internet
cloud.b: You can quickly use as much as you need. But because it lies outside the internal network boundary, access and data must be protected separately.

hybrid-cloud.s: A setup that uses the company's own servers and the cloud together
hybrid-cloud.b: Important systems stay in-house and the rest use the cloud. The challenge is applying the same security standards to both environments.

edge.s: Processing data close to the user or device
edge.b: It responds quickly because data does not have to travel to a distant central server.
